title: Breaking the glass
hookLine: a glass is broken to remember Jerusalem, even in joy

cards: A wedding feast in Babylonia, in the days of the Talmud. A rabbi named Mar, the son of Ravina, is marrying off his son. The guests are rabbis, and they're getting very merry.
Louder, and louder. So Mar brings out a precious cup, an expensive one, and breaks it right in front of them. The room changes.
The Talmud says they became serious. Something shifted in the middle of the joy, and that shift is today's custom.

teach.b: At the end of a Jewish wedding ceremony, a glass wrapped in cloth is set on the ground. The groom brings his foot down on it, and at some weddings both partners do.
A crunch, then the whole room shouts mazel tov, and the music starts. Tradition ties the broken glass to the destruction of Jerusalem and its Temple.
There's a Hebrew phrase for customs like this: zecher l'churban, a remembrance of the destruction. Psalm one hundred thirty-seven speaks in the voice of exiles by the rivers of Babylon.
In the King James words: "If I forget thee, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget her cunning." A verse later, the speaker vows to set Jerusalem "above my chief joy."
A wedding is a chief joy, so at that moment Jerusalem is set above it. In some communities those verses are said just before the glass is broken.
Mar's cup, though, wasn't mourning a city. He was keeping a party from forgetting itself. Later tradition joined the two ideas, and the custom holds both.
The glass doesn't cancel the joy: mazel tov comes right after the crash, not instead of it.
A happy couple and a loss still remembered share one room. Some add one more meaning: love, like glass, is precious and can break, so handle it with care.

how: At the end of a Jewish wedding ceremony, a glass wrapped in cloth is broken underfoot, traditionally by the groom and at some weddings by both partners, as a remembrance of Jerusalem's destruction; the guests then shout mazel tov.

o: a glass broken at a wedding to remember Jerusalem
a vow that the couple will never part, sealed in glass
a toast where every guest drinks from one cup

s: the glass is broken just for good luck
tradition ties it to remembering Jerusalem's destruction, even in joy.
the Talmud tells of a father breaking a costly cup at his son's wedding
Mar, son of Ravina, broke it when the rabbis grew too merry.
the broken glass ends the celebration

games.q: you're Mar, son of Ravina, at your son's wedding. the rabbis are getting merrier and louder. what do you do?
o: shout at them to calm down.
bring out a costly cup and break it in front of them.
games.why: he breaks a precious cup before them, and the Talmud says they became serious.

practice: Bring to mind something good, coming soon or just past, and let one person or place you've lost come to stand beside it, someone who would have been glad to be there.
Hold both at once, without choosing between them or rushing either: let the joy stay joy, and the memory stay memory.

wordCard.voice: Breaking the glass: a remembrance of Jerusalem at the height of a wedding, and then the shout of mazel tov. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: a remembrance of the destruction, of Jerusalem and its Temple.

carryVoice: Your line: joy and memory. One room is big enough for both of them. See you tomorrow.
